name: Scaling Mental Health Access Amid Workforce Shortages
shortDescription:
The demand for mental health services has risen sharply, particularly in the aftermath of war, displacement, trauma, and prolonged uncertainty. At the same time, healthcare systems are facing a severe shortage of psychologists, psychiatrists, and other qualified mental health professionals, creating long waiting times, limited access to care, and growing unmet need across communities. This challenge seeks scalable, practical, and equitable solutions that can expand access to mental health support despite workforce constraints.

We are looking for approaches that address the needs of diverse populations, including children, adolescents, adults, families, frontline workers, and vulnerable groups affected by acute and ongoing stress. Potential solutions may include new care models, digital tools, triage systems, community-based interventions, task shifting, prevention strategies, or methods for improving efficiency and continuity of care without compromising quality, safety, or trust.

This challenge is important because untreated mental health needs can have lasting effects on individuals, families, workplaces, and society. Future Of Health invites solvers to rethink how mental healthcare can be delivered at scale in times of crisis and recovery.
objective:
• People across affected communities can access timely, appropriate mental health support with significantly shorter wait times, fewer unmet needs, and clear pathways to higher levels of care when risk or complexity increases.
• Individuals, families, children, frontline workers, and vulnerable groups experience more consistent continuity of care, with support that is trusted, culturally relevant, and responsive across prevention, early intervention, crisis, and recovery settings.
• Existing care teams are able to serve more people safely and effectively, with reduced administrative burden, better prioritization of urgent cases, and clearer role allocation that protects quality while easing workforce strain and burnout.
• Mental health support becomes embedded within routine health, community, education, and workplace workflows, enabling smoother coordination, more reliable follow-up, and stronger connections between formal services and local support networks.
• Outcomes improve at individual and population level, demonstrated by earlier identification of need, better engagement and retention, reduced symptom escalation, fewer avoidable crises, and stronger functioning at home, school, work, and in community life.
• Health systems gain a scalable and equitable model for expanding access, with measurable improvements in coverage, efficiency, safety, and trust across diverse populations, including those historically underserved or affected by displacement, trauma, or prolonged stress.

name: Redesigning Healthcare Roles Through Technology
shortDescription:
Healthcare systems rely on a wide range of professional roles, from clinicians and care coordinators to administrative, operational, and support staff. Yet many of these roles were designed for a different era and may no longer reflect today’s clinical demands, workforce shortages, digital capabilities, or patient expectations. This challenge seeks ideas for how healthcare roles can be redefined, streamlined, or redistributed through the thoughtful use of technology, including automation, AI, digital workflows, decision support, and new models of collaboration.

We are looking for solutions that examine which tasks must remain human-led, which can be enhanced by technology, and which can be redesigned entirely to improve efficiency, quality, staff experience, and patient outcomes. Relevant audiences include hospitals, health systems, payers, public health organizations, and workforce leaders seeking practical, scalable change. The importance of this challenge lies in addressing burnout, rising costs, access constraints, and uneven care delivery. Strong responses should balance innovation with safety, ethics, workforce acceptance, and real-world implementation across diverse healthcare settings.
objective:
• Care teams operate with clearer role boundaries and more appropriate task allocation, allowing clinicians, coordinators, and support staff to spend more time on high-value work while reducing unnecessary handoffs, duplication, and delays across routine care and operational workflows.
• Staff experience measurably improves through lower administrative burden, reduced burnout risk, better workload balance, and stronger confidence in day-to-day responsibilities, leading to higher retention, faster onboarding into redesigned roles, and more sustainable workforce models across settings.
• Patients and members experience more timely, consistent, and coordinated services, with shorter wait times, fewer avoidable gaps in communication, and smoother navigation across care journeys, resulting in improved access, satisfaction, and continuity of care.
• Existing organizational processes absorb redesigned roles without disruption, with new responsibilities fitting naturally into care delivery, management, compliance, and reporting activities, and with teams able to work effectively across current systems, governance structures, and operational routines.
• Quality, safety, and accountability improve through better oversight of critical tasks, more reliable escalation pathways, fewer preventable errors, and clearer visibility into who is responsible for what, especially in complex, high-volume, or resource-constrained environments.
• Organizations gain measurable operational and financial value through higher productivity, more consistent service delivery, reduced avoidable labor costs, and new capacity to serve more people effectively without proportionally increasing staffing pressure.

name: Home-Based Health Monitoring for Families and Early Ear Care Detection
shortDescription:
Demand for healthier lifestyles and proactive self-care is rising rapidly, and consumers increasingly expect simple, reliable ways to monitor health from home. This challenge focuses on the growing need for accessible home-based tools that help individuals and families track health status, identify early signs of common conditions, and make informed decisions about when to seek professional care. A particularly important use case is monitoring children’s health at home, including early detection and follow-up of ear-related conditions such as ear infections, which are frequent, painful, and often difficult for parents to assess with confidence.

The target audience includes families, caregivers, parents of young children, and health-conscious individuals seeking convenient, trustworthy, and user-friendly solutions. The broader context is the shift toward preventive care, digital health adoption, and reducing unnecessary clinic visits while improving timely intervention when needed. This challenge matters because better at-home monitoring can empower families, improve patient experience, support earlier diagnosis, and create more connected, responsive models of care aligned with the future of health.
objective:
• Families and caregivers can confidently assess day-to-day health changes at home and act earlier, leading to faster recognition of concerning symptoms, more appropriate care-seeking decisions, and less uncertainty when managing common childhood conditions such as ear-related discomfort.
• Routine home monitoring becomes a trusted part of family health behavior, improving adherence to observation, follow-up, and symptom tracking while reducing missed warning signs, unnecessary anxiety, and avoidable delays between first symptoms and clinical attention.
• Clinicians receive clearer, more consistent information from households, enabling better triage, more informed consultations, and more timely intervention, while reducing avoidable in-person visits and ensuring higher-risk cases are identified and escalated sooner.
• Health data from home settings fits naturally into existing care pathways and communication workflows, allowing parents, caregivers, and care teams to share a common view of symptoms, progress, and next steps without adding friction to routine healthcare interactions.
• Success is demonstrated by measurable gains in early identification, reduced inappropriate clinic utilization, improved follow-up compliance, and stronger caregiver confidence, alongside better patient experience and lower burden on frontline services.
• Value is created across the system: children experience quicker relief and fewer complications, families gain reassurance and practical decision support, care teams work more efficiently, and health organizations strengthen preventive, connected, and responsive models of care.

name: Early Detection of Hypertension in the Workplace
shortDescription:
How can large employers identify common but often undiagnosed conditions such as hypertension among employees early enough to improve health outcomes, reduce long-term complications, and support a healthier workforce? Many workers do not routinely monitor blood pressure or engage with preventive care, especially in fast-paced, high-pressure environments where symptoms may go unnoticed until serious health issues emerge. This challenge seeks practical, scalable, and privacy-conscious solutions that help organizations detect risk, increase awareness, and connect employees to appropriate follow-up care without creating stigma or unnecessary burden.

The target audience includes large enterprises, occupational health teams, benefits leaders, insurers, digital health innovators, and public health experts. Proposed solutions should consider diverse employee populations, different work settings, and varying levels of health literacy and access to care. The challenge is important because hypertension is a major risk factor for heart disease, stroke, and other chronic conditions, yet it is highly manageable when identified early. Future Of Health is looking for approaches that combine prevention, engagement, and operational feasibility to create measurable impact at workforce scale.
objective:
• Employees across office, remote, field, and shift-based settings routinely identify elevated blood pressure earlier, increasing the share of previously undiagnosed individuals who receive timely clinical follow-up before serious complications develop.
• Preventive health behaviors become part of normal workforce routines, with higher participation in screening, stronger awareness of personal cardiovascular risk, and improved follow-through on recommended next steps without stigma or excessive effort.
• Occupational health, benefits, and people teams gain a dependable workflow for monitoring population-level risk trends, triaging support, and coordinating referrals within existing wellbeing, insurance, and employee health processes.
• Success is reflected in measurable reductions in uncontrolled hypertension, avoidable cardiovascular events, emergency claims, and long-term health risk exposure, alongside improved clinical engagement and earlier intervention across the employee population.
• Employers are able to support workforce health at scale while protecting trust, with equitable reach across diverse employee groups, locations, job types, and health literacy levels, ensuring value for individuals and the wider organization.
• The organization develops a sustained capability to act on workforce health insights, enabling better planning, lower absence and productivity loss, and a stronger prevention model that can extend to other chronic conditions over time.
rewardInformation: Future Of Health is prepared to award a paid pilot opportunity to the strongest submission, with an anticipated budget of USD 40,000-80,000 for a solution that can be deployed within 3 months and demonstrates clear potential for workforce-scale impact. Additional consideration will be given for follow-on commercial engagement, including implementation support or multi-site rollout, for solutions that show strong privacy safeguards, measurable detection outcomes, employee engagement, and operational fit for large employers.

name: Medication administration
shortDescription: Medication administration errors remain a critical challenge across hospitals, rehabilitation centers, long-term care, and homecare settings. This challenge focuses on ensuring that each dose is given to the right patient, at the right time, and exactly as prescribed, while minimizing disruption to clinical workflows. We are seeking solutions that can reliably confirm both patient identity and medication match at the point of administration, reducing the risk of mix-ups, missed doses, and preventable adverse events. The target users include nurses, caregivers, and healthcare staff who operate in fast-paced environments where efficiency, accuracy, and ease of use are essential. The ideal approach should add minimal burden to frontline teams, work in real-world care settings, and help improve compliance, safety, and confidence for patients, providers, and families. We are particularly interested in solutions that are clinically grounded, safe, ethically responsible, and realistic for future implementation in healthcare settings. name: Connecting the Full Patient Picture Through Integrated Health Data
shortDescription:
Today, vast amounts of health information are generated across the patient journey, from wellness and prevention data to clinical records, diagnostics, medications, symptoms, and treatment histories. Yet this information often remains fragmented across systems, providers, and specialties. As a result, no single clinician consistently connects the full picture of a person’s health, making it difficult to identify patterns, understand interactions between conditions, or make truly holistic care decisions.

This challenge seeks solutions that can help integrate and interpret diverse health data into a more comprehensive view of the patient. The target audience includes innovators in digital health, clinical decision support, AI, data interoperability, and patient-centered care. The goal is to enable care teams to move beyond isolated symptoms or single-disease management toward a deeper, more connected understanding of overall health status. Solving this problem is critical to improving diagnosis, personalization of care, prevention, and long-term outcomes across increasingly complex healthcare systems.
objective:
• Clinicians, care coordinators, and allied health teams operate from a shared, longitudinal view of each person’s health, reducing blind spots and enabling faster, more accurate decisions across prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up.
• Care decisions consistently reflect interactions across conditions, medications, tests, symptoms, and lifestyle factors, leading to measurable improvements in diagnostic confidence, personalization of care plans, and earlier identification of avoidable risks.
• Existing workflows become more coordinated and efficient, with less time spent searching across disconnected records, fewer duplicate tests or conflicting actions, and smoother handoffs between specialties, settings, and points of care.
• Patients experience more coherent, continuous care, with fewer requests to repeat their history, greater confidence that providers understand their full situation, and more timely interventions that improve outcomes and long-term health management.
• Health organizations gain new capabilities to identify trends across populations, stratify risk more effectively, and target preventive or proactive care models, improving resource allocation, quality performance, and equity of access and outcomes.
• Success is evidenced by reduced care fragmentation, lower avoidable utilization, improved safety and continuity measures, stronger multidisciplinary collaboration, and routine use of the complete patient picture in everyday clinical and operational decision-making.

name: Food-Grade Bulking Solutions for Sugar-Reduced Chocolate
shortDescription:

Reducing sugar in chocolate is not only a nutritional challenge, but also a structural one, since sugar contributes significantly to bulk, particle interactions, viscosity, mouthfeel, sweetness balance, and final texture. The goal of this challenge is to identify filler solutions that can replace part of the sugar mass without introducing off-flavors, excessive cooling effects, instability, or undesirable changes during refining, conching, tempering, molding, and storage.

We are looking for approaches relevant to chocolate developers, ingredient suppliers, food technologists, and material innovators that can support smooth processing and deliver a final product with acceptable snap, gloss, melt profile, and creamy texture. name: Smart Municipal Solutions to Reduce Urban Traffic Congestion
shortDescription:
Road congestion in Israel has become a persistent urban challenge, while the physical ability to expand road infrastructure is limited by land constraints, cost, environmental considerations, and the need to preserve quality of life in growing cities such as Modiin. As a result, municipalities and residents face increasing traffic jams, longer travel times, unreliable public transportation, reduced road safety, higher emissions, and ongoing economic loss caused by delays and inefficiency.

This challenge seeks practical, scalable solutions that can help reduce congestion without relying on major road expansion. Relevant approaches may include smarter traffic management, data-driven planning, demand regulation, mobility behavior change, improved coordination between transport modes, and tools that support better decision-making for municipalities and the public. The target audience includes technology providers, mobility experts, researchers, planners, startups, and multidisciplinary teams with experience in urban transportation and smart city solutions.

The goal is to identify solutions that can be adapted to real municipal conditions, improve traffic flow, and create measurable benefits for residents, commuters, and city operations. This issue is especially important because congestion affects daily life, accessibility, sustainability, and the long-term resilience of urban transportation systems.

• Municipal traffic, planning, and operations teams work from a consistent citywide view of mobility conditions, enabling faster coordination, better prioritization of interventions, and routine use of mobility insights in daily management and long-term planning.
• Road users adopt more balanced travel patterns across routes, times, and modes, reducing pressure on chronic bottlenecks and improving overall network performance without requiring major expansion of physical road capacity.
• Safety conditions improve at congested intersections and high-conflict corridors, with fewer risky interactions, reduced incident-related disruption, and better protection for pedestrians, cyclists, drivers, and public transport users.
• The municipality gains measurable operational and environmental benefits, including lower congestion-related emissions, more efficient use of existing infrastructure, reduced economic loss from delay, and a stronger ability to maintain quality of life as the city grows.

name: Safe Early Mobility for Hospitalized Older Adults
shortDescription:
We are seeking a solution to a common and significant problem among hospitalized patients, especially older adults: functional decline during admission due to prolonged bed rest and limited mobility. Many patients arrive at the hospital relatively independent and ambulatory, but after several days of illness, inactivity, and extended time in bed, they lose strength, balance, and confidence. Clinical evidence shows that early, supervised mobilization is essential for maintaining function, reducing fall risk, shortening recovery time, and improving overall outcomes. However, hospitals often lack the staffing needed to support this consistently. There are not enough physiotherapists or trained personnel available to safely monitor walking and mobility exercises for every patient who would benefit.

The challenge is to develop a practical, scalable solution that helps hospitalized patients get out of bed and walk safely under supervision, even in settings with limited manpower. The target users are mainly older inpatients and the care teams responsible for their recovery. An effective solution could improve patient safety, preserve independence, reduce complications of immobility, and ease the burden on overstretched hospital staff.

In the desired future state, eligible patients are mobilized earlier and more consistently, helping them maintain strength, balance, confidence, and functional independence throughout hospitalization. Success will be reflected in measurable improvements such as higher walking-accompaniment rates, reduced functional decline, fewer mobility-related complications, lower fall risk during recovery, and smoother discharge readiness. The improved model should fit naturally into daily ward operations, enabling nursing teams, physiotherapy staff, and other caregivers to coordinate mobility support within existing clinical workflows and patient care plans. Value will be created at multiple levels: patients retain more independence, care teams can support mobility more reliably despite workload constraints, and the organization benefits from safer care, better outcomes, and more efficient use of staff resources.

This challenge focuses on identifying effective, scalable solutions that can strengthen connection, improve emotional wellbeing, and support healthy aging for people in later life. The target audience includes seniors living independently, in assisted living settings, or within underserved communities, as well as caregivers, families, and health systems that support them. Loneliness in older age is not only a social issue but also a major health concern, linked to depression, cognitive decline, worsening physical health, and increased healthcare utilization. Addressing this problem requires cross-sector thinking that combines community support, digital inclusion, service design, and preventive health approaches. FOH Future Of Health seeks ideas that can help build more connected, dignified, and resilient lives for aging populations.
objective: Success will mean that older adults experience a sustained increase in meaningful social connection, stronger emotional wellbeing, and greater day-to-day participation in community and care environments. In the desired end state, risks related to loneliness are identified earlier, supportive actions become part of routine operations, and engagement is no longer treated as an optional add-on but as a core component of healthy aging. Caregivers, assisted living teams, community partners, and health systems work in a coordinated way, using existing touchpoints to connect individuals to relevant support and activities. Success will be visible through measurable reductions in reported loneliness and social isolation, improved wellbeing and quality-of-life indicators, higher participation and retention in social programs, fewer avoidable escalations linked to mental or physical decline, and more efficient use of staff time through clearer pathways for referral and follow-up. Value is created for older adults, families, frontline teams, provider organizations, and the broader health system.

name: Innovating Better Toothbrushing Habits for Children
shortDescription:
Tooth decay remains one of the most common health challenges among children aged 4 and above, yet encouraging consistent and effective toothbrushing continues to be difficult for many families and caregivers. The issue is not only whether children brush their teeth, but how they brush: many do not use the correct technique, brush for too short a time, or miss key areas, reducing the effectiveness of daily oral care. This challenge is relevant to children, parents, educators, pediatric dental professionals, and public health organizations seeking practical ways to improve oral hygiene habits early in life.

The need is for solutions that help children understand, enjoy, and adopt proper brushing behavior in a sustained way. Effective approaches should address motivation, habit formation, technique guidance, and age-appropriate engagement. Early intervention is critical, as poor oral health in childhood can lead to pain, infection, missed school days, long-term dental problems, and increased healthcare costs. FOH Future Of Health is seeking innovative ideas that can make correct toothbrushing more accessible, engaging, and measurable for young children, with the potential to create lasting health impact at scale.
objective: Success will mean that children regularly complete effective toothbrushing as a normal part of daily life, with clear improvement in brushing duration, coverage, and technique across home, school, and care settings. Parents and caregivers will spend less time prompting or correcting and more time reinforcing positive routines, while educators and pediatric oral health professionals can support consistent messages and behaviors through existing health, wellness, and preventive care activities. FOH Future Of Health seeks an end state in which better brushing habits are sustained over time, progress can be measured reliably, and oral hygiene support becomes easier to embed into everyday workflows rather than treated as a separate intervention. Success will be reflected in higher adherence rates, stronger habit retention, fewer missed brushing moments, improved oral health indicators, reduced risk of preventable decay, and lower downstream burden on families and health systems. Value is created for children through healthier outcomes, for caregivers through reduced friction, for professionals through better visibility and coordination, and for public health organizations through scalable, measurable impact.

name: Reducing Administrative Burden to Improve Physician Efficiency and Care Delivery
shortDescription:
Many healthcare providers operate under extreme daily pressure caused by a combination of clinical overload and administrative inefficiency. Physicians are expected to deliver high-quality care while also dealing with appointment scheduling, patient flow, cancellations, no-shows, billing, collections, and ongoing operational coordination. When these systems are poorly managed or fragmented, the result is a stressful environment that wastes valuable clinical time, reduces revenue capture, and increases burnout across the organization.

This challenge is aimed at innovators who can address the intersection of care delivery and practice operations for clinics, medical groups, and independent physicians. The goal is to identify practical solutions that improve scheduling accuracy, streamline payment collection, reduce administrative friction, and enable physicians to focus more of their time on patients rather than process management. This issue is especially important in a healthcare environment facing staff shortages, rising costs, and growing patient demand. Solving it can improve financial sustainability, operational efficiency, staff wellbeing, and ultimately the quality and continuity of care.
objective: Success will mean physicians consistently spend more of their working day on direct patient care and clinical decision-making, while routine operational work is handled accurately, predictably, and with far less manual intervention. Appointment capacity is used more effectively, patient flow is smoother, cancellations and no-shows create less disruption, and billing and collections happen with fewer delays, errors, and missed opportunities. Front-desk, administrative, and clinical teams operate from a shared, reliable workflow that fits naturally into existing practice routines and supports better coordination across scheduling, visits, follow-up, and financial processes. At the individual level, staff experience lower stress, fewer repetitive tasks, and clearer accountability. At the organizational level, success is reflected in improved physician productivity, stronger revenue capture, faster cycle times, reduced administrative overhead, and lower burnout-related risk. Patients benefit from more timely access, fewer friction points, and a more consistent care experience. In the ideal end state, practices gain a sustainable operating model that improves care quality, workforce wellbeing, and financial resilience at the same time.

name: Early Intervention for Anxiety in Wartime Settings
shortDescription:
During periods of war and prolonged insecurity, many people who usually function well in daily life may begin to experience anxiety, emotional distress, sleep disruption, irritability, difficulty concentrating, or reduced ability to cope. In many cases, these individuals do not meet the threshold for acute psychiatric care, yet they may still benefit from timely, light-touch support that can prevent further deterioration. The challenge is to identify practical, accessible, and scalable ways to provide early intervention for people with emerging anxiety symptoms before their condition worsens.

This challenge is relevant for civilians, families, workers, students, and community members exposed to ongoing stress, uncertainty, and threat. It is especially important for health systems and communities seeking solutions that are low-barrier, culturally sensitive, and easy to deploy in crisis settings. By addressing anxiety early, it may be possible to reduce long-term mental health burden, strengthen resilience, and preserve everyday functioning during and after wartime conditions.

Individuals will recognize distress sooner, seek support earlier, and uset feel safe, relevant, and easy to access. Frontline teams, employers, educators, community organizations, and health services will operate with clearer referral and support routines, allowing mild to moderate needs to be addressed consistently before they intensify. Existing care pathways will be better coordinated, with fewer gaps between self-care, community support, and formal services. At an organizational level, success will be reflected in reduced avoidable deterioration, lower demand on emergency and specialist mental health resources, faster identification of at-risk populations, and improved continuity of care during disruption. Value will be created for individuals through improved coping and resilience, for teams through clearer workflows and reduced burden, and for health systems through greater preventive capacity, efficiency, and readiness in prolonged crisis conditions.

shortDescription: Healthcare organizations repeatedly face the need to train clinical and operational teams each time a new digital system is introduced, whether for electronic records, workflow management, diagnostics, communication, or patient engagement. This challenge focuses on how to make these training processes more effective, scalable, and less disruptive in complex care environments. The target audience includes physicians, nurses, allied health professionals, administrators, and support staff who must quickly adopt new tools while maintaining high standards of care, safety, and efficiency. In many cases, implementation succeeds technically but falls short operationally because users are not sufficiently prepared, engaged, or supported during the transition. This creates resistance, inconsistent usage, lower productivity, and potential risks to patient outcomes. The need is therefore not only for training, but for smarter onboarding approaches that improve confidence, accelerate adoption, and ensure new systems deliver real value across diverse healthcare settings.

name: Advancing Interoperable Health Data Exchange Across the Care Ecosystem
shortDescription:
Connecting data between hospitals, clinics, and other care providers across the United States remains one of the most persistent barriers to better healthcare delivery. Patient information is often fragmented across disconnected systems, vendors, and formats, making it difficult to create a complete, timely, and accurate view of an individual’s health journey. This challenge is especially relevant for health systems, ambulatory networks, payers, digital health companies, and policymakers seeking to improve care coordination, reduce duplication, and support better clinical and operational decisions.

The problem extends beyond technical interoperability alone. It includes inconsistent standards, regulatory complexity, privacy concerns, legacy infrastructure, and limited incentives for seamless data sharing. As a result, clinicians may lack critical information at the point of care, patients face repeated tests and administrative friction, and organizations struggle to generate actionable insights at scale. FOH Future Of Health is seeking solutions that can help bridge these gaps and enable secure, efficient, and meaningful data exchange across the care ecosystem, with the goal of improving outcomes, experience, and system-wide efficiency.

Clinicians will spend less time searching for records, repeating documentation, or making decisions with incomplete context, and more time delivering coordinated, informed care. Patients will experience fewer duplicate tests, smoother transitions between settings, and less administrative burden. Care teams, operational leaders, and partner organizations will be able to use shared information within existing workflows to support referrals, discharge planning, utilization management, quality improvement, and population health efforts. name: Hospital Energy Efficiency and Sustainability Challenge
shortDescription:
Hospitals are among the most energy-intensive facilities in any community, operating 24/7 and relying on complex systems such as HVAC, lighting, medical equipment, sterilization, refrigeration, data infrastructure, and backup power. This challenge seeks practical, scalable solutions to reduce hospital energy consumption without compromising patient safety, clinical quality, infection control, or operational continuity. The target audience includes innovators, health system leaders, energy specialists, engineers, facility managers, digital health companies, and sustainability experts who can address both immediate efficiency gains and long-term transformation.

The need is urgent. Rising energy costs, pressure to reduce carbon emissions, and growing expectations for resilient health systems are forcing hospitals to rethink how they consume and manage energy. Yet many hospitals struggle with aging infrastructure, fragmented data, and limited capital for large upgrades. We are looking for ideas, technologies, business models, and implementation approaches that can measurably improve efficiency, optimize resource use, and support more sustainable hospital operations. Successful solutions should be feasible in real-world healthcare environments and demonstrate clear environmental, financial, and operational value.

Existing workflows, asset management, maintenance planning, and financial oversight are strengthened by clearer visibility, faster response to inefficiencies, and more proactive resource allocation. Success will be evident through measurable reductions in energy consumption, peak demand, avoidable operating costs, and carbon footprint, alongside improved resilience, fewer system failures, and stronger continuity during periods of stress. name: Improving Patient Wayfinding in Hospital Environments
shortDescription:
Patients arriving at hospitals often struggle to locate the exact department, clinic, testing unit, or treatment area they need to reach. Large, complex hospital campuses can be difficult to navigate, especially for first-time visitors, elderly patients, people with disabilities, non-native speakers, or individuals under stress. Confusing layouts, unclear signage, last-minute schedule changes, and limited staff availability for guidance can lead to delays, missed appointments, increased anxiety, and reduced operational efficiency.

This challenge seeks innovative solutions that improve wayfinding within hospital environments and help patients reach their destination quickly, confidently, and independently. The target audience includes patients, family members, caregivers, and visitors across a wide range of care settings, from outpatient clinics to inpatient services and diagnostic centers. Solving this problem is important not only for patient experience, but also for access, safety, workflow, and the overall quality of care delivery in modern health systems.

Wayfinding becomes fully aligned with day-to-day hospital operations, reflecting real patient flows, schedule changes, accessibility needs, and multilingual communication requirements. name: Improving Access and Follow-Up in Menopause Care
shortDescription:

A major barrier is the need to update clinical protocols and care pathways as symptoms evolve and treatment responses vary over time. As a result, patients may experience delays in receiving hormone therapy, symptom management support, and routine monitoring, which can negatively affect quality of life, adherence, and long-term health outcomes.

This challenge is relevant to healthcare providers, health systems, digital health innovators, and policymakers seeking to improve continuity of care for midlife women. The problem sits at the intersection of women’s health, care access, protocol design, and care coordination. There is a clear need for scalable solutions that enable more flexible follow-up, smarter protocol updates, and easier access to prescribing clinicians while maintaining safety and clinical oversight. Addressing this gap is essential to creating more responsive, equitable, and patient-centered menopause care.

shortDescription:

This challenge seeks solutions that address the gap between vaccine eligibility and actual vaccination among adolescents.

The target audience includes public health leaders, school systems, healthcare providers, community organizations, policymakers, and innovators working to improve preventive care for young people. The context may include school-based vaccination programs, community clinics, and national immunization campaigns where consent processes create friction and delay. Improving adolescent vaccine acceptance is important not only for protecting individual health, but also for strengthening population immunity, reducing preventable disease burden, and ensuring more equitable access to care across diverse communities.

name: Safe Hospital-to-Home Care in War and Emergency Settings
shortDescription:
How can healthcare systems safely discharge patients for continued treatment at home during times of war and large-scale emergency? In conflict settings, hospitals face extreme pressure from rising demand, limited staff, infrastructure disruption, security risks, and shortages of beds, equipment, and transportation. At the same time, many patients still require ongoing clinical monitoring, rehabilitation, medication management, oxygen support, mental health care, or follow-up after acute treatment. This challenge seeks practical, scalable solutions that enable earlier and safer transition from hospital to home without compromising quality of care or patient safety.

The target audience includes hospitals, health systems, home care providers, digital health innovators, emergency planners, and community-based organizations. Solutions should address care coordination, remote monitoring, caregiver support, discharge planning, continuity of treatment, and rapid response if a patient’s condition worsens. The goal is to strengthen health system resilience, reduce unnecessary hospital occupancy, and ensure that vulnerable patients can continue receiving appropriate care in the community when hospital capacity is under severe strain.
objective: Success means hospitals can transition appropriate patients to home-based care during conflict or large-scale emergencies without loss of safety, continuity, or clinical oversight. In the desired end state, discharge decisions are consistent, coordinated, and embedded in routine operations across hospital teams, community providers, caregivers, and emergency response partners. Patients continue receiving the right level of treatment, monitoring, rehabilitation, medication support, and follow-up at home, while signs of deterioration are identified early and acted on quickly. This results in fewer avoidable readmissions, fewer adverse events after discharge, shorter unnecessary hospital stays, and better use of scarce beds, staff time, transport, and critical equipment. Success also means caregivers are better prepared, responsibilities are clear, and information flows reliably across settings despite disruption. Value is created at every level: patients experience safer recovery and greater continuity of care, care teams work with clearer pathways and less fragmentation, health systems improve surge capacity and resilience, and communities gain a stronger, more dependable model for sustaining care outside the hospital.

name: Ensuring Continuity of Care at Home Following Crisis-Driven Early Discharge
shortDescription:
During times of war or national emergency, hospitals may be unable to admit patients to their regular departments due to security constraints, overload, staff shortages, or the urgent need to reserve capacity for trauma and critical care. As a result, many patients who would normally remain hospitalized for monitoring, recovery, or continued treatment must be discharged earlier than clinically ideal and continue care at home. This creates a major challenge for health systems, care teams, patients, and families: how to ensure safe, effective, and equitable continuity of care outside the hospital under unstable and resource-constrained conditions.

This challenge seeks solutions for recently discharged patients who still require medical supervision, rehabilitation, medication management, symptom monitoring, or rapid escalation if their condition worsens. Relevant populations may include older adults, patients with chronic illness, post-acute patients, and individuals with limited caregiver support. The goal is to identify models, tools, and services that can reduce readmissions, prevent deterioration, support caregivers, and maintain quality of care when inpatient capacity is disrupted. This is a critical resilience issue for modern health systems facing conflict, crisis, and prolonged instability.
objective: Success will mean that patients discharged home during periods of severe system disruption continue to receive coordinated, safe, and effective care without avoidable decline. In the ideal end state, post-discharge follow-up, medication adherence, symptom surveillance, rehabilitation support, and escalation pathways operate as a seamless extension of routine clinical care, embedded into existing hospital, community, and primary care workflows. Care teams can identify deterioration earlier, prioritize higher-risk patients, and act consistently across settings, while patients and caregivers know what to do, whom to contact, and when urgent intervention is needed. Measurable success includes fewer preventable readmissions, adverse events, and missed follow-ups; faster response to clinical deterioration; improved continuity across handoffs; and more efficient use of inpatient capacity during crisis periods. Value is created for patients through safer recovery at home, for caregivers through greater confidence and lower burden, for clinicians through clearer coordination and decision-making, and for health systems through stronger resilience, more equitable access to support, and sustained quality of care under pressure.
